title: Ethan Frome
author: Edith Wharton
written: Out of an earlier French exercise, Hiver, written while Wharton was living in Paris
setting: Starkfield, a declining Massachusetts hill village, across one winter and twenty-four years later
lengthNote: A prologue, nine short chapters and an epilogue — under two hundred pages
openingLine: I had the story, bit by bit, from various people, and, as generally happens in such cases, each time it was a different story.
summary: An engineer stranded by a strike in a New England village becomes curious about a lame, silent man at the post office, and assembles the reason from what the neighbours will tell him. What he arrives at is a winter twenty-four years earlier, a farm that cannot be sold, a wife with symptoms and a young cousin with nowhere else to go. The cruelty of the book lies in what the accident at the end fails to end.
referenceStyle: chapter — the framing narrative is unnumbered and is referenced here as Prologue and Epilogue

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Ethan Frome
sourceText.note: Chapters are numbered I to IX, with Wharton's unnumbered opening and closing sections given here as Prologue and Epilogue. The phonetic Starkfield speech is reproduced as printed.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: By Charles Scribner's Sons, after serialisation in Scribner's Magazine.

atAGlance.label: Written first in French
atAGlance.note: A composition exercise Wharton wrote while living in Paris supplied the situation and the setting.

atAGlance.label: Time span
atAGlance.note: The distance between the winter the narrator reconstructs and the kitchen he finally walks into.

atAGlance.label: Narration
atAGlance.note: Everything between the prologue and the epilogue is what the engineer has made of other people's fragments.

structure.label: Prologue
structure.title: The narrator comes to Starkfield
structure.summary: Held in Starkfield by a carpenters' strike, the narrator notices a ruined man at the post office and starts asking. Harmon Gow supplies the accident, Mrs Ned Hale supplies a reticence, and a snowstorm finally puts him inside the Frome kitchen — at which point the book goes back twenty-four years.

structure.label: Chapters I–III
structure.title: Waiting outside the dance
structure.summary: Ethan stands in the cold watching Mattie Silver dance with Denis Eady, and walks her home the long way past the graveyard. Zeena is awake when they get in, and by the third chapter she has announced a trip to Bettsbridge to see a new doctor.

structure.label: Chapters IV–V
structure.title: An evening alone, and the cat breaks the dish
structure.summary: With Zeena away, Ethan and Mattie have supper in a kitchen that briefly feels like a different life. The cat knocks Zeena's red glass pickle-dish off the table, and Ethan puts the pieces back on the shelf intending to buy glue in the morning.

structure.label: Chapters VI–VII
structure.title: Zeena’s return, and the broken dish found
structure.summary: Zeena comes back with a diagnosis and a hired girl already engaged, which means Mattie must leave in the morning. Ethan has no money and no argument, and when the pieces of the dish are discovered the quarrel stops being about anybody's health.

structure.label: Chapters VIII–IX
structure.title: Mattie leaves, and the sled ride
structure.summary: Ethan drafts a letter he cannot send, goes to Andrew Hale for an advance he does not get, and drives Mattie to the station by way of the sledding hill. She asks him not to leave her, and then asks him for something else.

structure.label: Epilogue
structure.title: The kitchen, twenty-four years on
structure.summary: The narrator is shown into the room the three of them share, and the two women in it are not arranged as anyone would have predicted. Mrs Hale afterwards says the thing nobody in Starkfield has said aloud for a quarter of a century.

characters.name: Ethan Frome
characters.role: A farmer and sawmill owner, twenty-eight in the reconstructed winter
characters.summary: He studied engineering for a year at Worcester and came back to nurse first his father, then his mother, then the wife he married because the silence after his mother's funeral was unbearable. Every exit is costed in the book and none of them clears: he cannot sell the farm, cannot raise fifty dollars, and cannot leave without abandoning a sick woman.
characters.clue: A lame man with a red gash across his forehead who drives into the village every day at noon for a newspaper he never opens.

characters.name: Zenobia (Zeena) Frome
characters.role: Ethan's wife, seven years older than him
characters.summary: She came to nurse his mother and stayed as his wife, and her illness — never diagnosed by the book — is the only authority a woman in her position has. Wharton gives her almost no interior life and a great deal of power, and the epilogue reverses the two so completely that the reader has to reconsider everything said about her.
characters.clue: She goes to a new doctor in a neighbouring town and comes home with a word that outranks trouble, and a hired girl already engaged.

characters.name: Mattie Silver
characters.role: Zeena's young cousin, working in the house for her keep
characters.summary: Her father's failure left her with fifty dollars and no training; shop work and stenography both broke her health, so she is at the Fromes because there is nowhere else. She is not a great beauty or a great mind — the novel is careful about that — she is simply the only warm thing in the house.
characters.clue: She hangs a ribbon at her neck, uses the good dish for one supper, and asks at the top of a hill to be steered at a tree.

characters.name: The engineer
characters.role: An unnamed visitor sent to Corbury Junction on a job
characters.summary: He is never named and never explains his own life, and he states at the outset that the story came to him in pieces that did not agree. The central chapters are his construction, not testimony, which means every judgement the reader makes about Zeena arrives through a stranger who spent one night in the house.

characters.name: Harmon Gow
characters.role: Former driver of the Bettsbridge stage
characters.summary: He knew the families along the route before the trolley and the railway came, and he gives the narrator the accident, the dates and the single sentence on which the whole reconstruction rests. His information stops exactly where the village's sympathy stops.

characters.name: Mrs Ned Hale
characters.role: The narrator's landlady, formerly Ruth Varnum
characters.summary: She was the first person into the house after the accident and has said almost nothing about it since. Her reticence is what gives the epilogue its force: when she finally speaks she delivers the harshest verdict in the book, and immediately apologises for it.

characters.name: Andrew Hale
characters.summary: He pays for lumber three months after delivery and is himself short of money because he is fitting out a house for his son's marriage. His refusal of an advance is delivered kindly and is the exact point at which every remaining exit closes.

characters.name: Denis Eady
characters.role: The grocer's son, with his father's horses to drive
characters.summary: He has money, a cutter and no obligations, which makes him the version of Ethan's life that was available to somebody else. He offers Mattie a lift home from the dance and is refused, and afterwards he functions mainly as the future the Fromes cannot compete with.

themes.name: Class and money
themes.summary: The book gives exact figures and lets them do the work of fate: fifty dollars asked for and refused, lumber paid for three months in arrears, a mortgage that cannot be cleared, a girl with no saleable skill. Wharton’s tragedy is a matter of a household that cannot raise the fare out, more than of temperament.
themes.development: The poverty is scenery in the early chapters and machinery by Chapter VIII, where the plan to run away collapses on the price of the tickets.

themes.name: Duty and the sick wife
themes.summary: Ethan is held by illness: first his father’s, then his mother’s, then Zeena’s, in an unbroken line of people who need nursing. The novel never says whether Zeena is ill or has discovered that illness is the only authority open to her, and that silence is the point.
themes.development: Marriage is presented as the consequence of a funeral, and the epilogue completes the pattern by putting the invalid on her feet to nurse the girl she sent away.

themes.name: Silence
themes.summary: Almost nothing in this book is spoken at the moment it matters. Ethan rehearses sentences he does not deliver, writes a letter he does not send, and says goodbye without saying anything; Mrs Ned Hale keeps her verdict for twenty-four years. Wharton makes the unspoken sentence a physical event, with a place in the scene.
themes.development: The narrator names the silence in the prologue as something frozen; by Chapter IX the two people involved can reach each other only by what they do.

themes.name: Winter
themes.summary: Cold in this book is economics: it decides what work can be done, which roads are passable, how long it takes to reach the station and what a farm can earn. The village’s phrase for a man ruined by staying, too many winters, is a piece of local economics.
themes.development: The narrator experiences one winter and finds it merely severe; the reconstruction shows what twenty-eight of them do, and the epilogue confines all three survivors to a single heated kitchen.

themes.name: Love and harm
themes.summary: The feeling between Ethan and Mattie is made of very small things — a ribbon, a chair moved, a shared supper — and the novel is precise about how little it would have taken to satisfy it and how completely that little is unavailable. What it produces is an attempt at a double suicide that leaves both of them alive.
themes.development: It begins as company in Chapter I, becomes a domestic fantasy over one supper, and by the top of the sledding hill has turned into the conviction that there is no version of being together except not surviving.

themes.name: Isolation
themes.summary: Starkfield is described as a place where the clever leave and the rest are snowed in, and the Frome farm stands a mile beyond even that. The house has had a wing pulled down, which the narrator reads as the look of a body with a limb missing, and the epilogue shuts three people into one room with nobody to overhear them.
themes.development: Geographic at first, then social — nobody visits — and finally absolute, when the only stranger to enter the kitchen in years is a man waiting out a storm.

techniques.name: Frame narrative
techniques.definition: A story enclosed within another story, often several layers deep.
techniques.inThisBook: The prologue and epilogue belong to an outsider who admits his sources contradicted each other; the nine chapters between them are his reconstruction, given with a confidence about Ethan's private thoughts that no informant could have supplied.

techniques.name: Landscape
techniques.definition: Using terrain, weather and scale to act on the characters, not to decorate them.
techniques.inThisBook: The hill, the snow, the distance to Corbury Flats and the elm at the bottom of the run are all load-bearing: each of them limits what a character is physically able to do next.

techniques.name: Dialect
techniques.inThisBook: The villagers' speech is set down as it sounds — 'wust kind', ''cept', 'ha' died' — while the narrator's prose stays formal, so the gap between the observer and the observed is audible on every page he quotes.

techniques.name: Objects and omens
techniques.definition: Things in the narrative that carry a meaning the characters half-register.
techniques.inThisBook: A wedding-present pickle-dish taken down for one supper and broken by a cat carries the whole marriage; so do a hanging ribbon, a dead cucumber-vine and a gravestone with the wrong first name on it.

techniques.name: Omission
techniques.definition: Leaving out the part of a story the reader most expects to be shown.
techniques.inThisBook: The novel jumps from a sled aimed at an elm to a kitchen twenty-four years later without narrating the crash, the injuries or the decisions afterwards, so the reader reconstructs the worst of it from a woman's shape in a chair.

techniques.name: Understatement
techniques.definition: Reporting extreme events in language deliberately too mild for them.
techniques.inThisBook: The village calls a catastrophe a smash-up, a driver says Ethan will likely touch a hundred, and the book's cruellest judgement is delivered by a kindly landlady who then worries she has spoken out of turn.

quotations.text: I had the story, bit by bit, from various people, and, as generally happens in such cases, each time it was a different story.
quotations.speaker: The narrator
quotations.context: The opening sentence of the book.
quotations.analysis: The first sentence of a tragedy is a warning about evidence. 'Bit by bit' concedes that the pieces arrived separately, and the last clause concedes that they contradicted each other — so everything the reader is about to be shown in close-up third person has been assembled by a man who has just told us his materials do not agree.

quotations.text: He’s looked that way ever since he had his smash-up; and that’s twenty-four years ago come next February
quotations.speaker: Harmon Gow
quotations.context: The first explanation the narrator is offered for Frome's appearance.
quotations.analysis: The village's word for the event is a word for a cart overturning, and the sentence dates it with the precision people use for a wedding or a death. The whole book is contained in the gap between the mildness of 'smash-up' and the fact that somebody has been counting the Februaries.

quotations.text: He looks as if he was dead and in hell now!
quotations.speaker: Harmon Gow
quotations.context: Answering his own remark that Frome will probably live to a hundred.
quotations.analysis: Gow has just said the Fromes are tough and will last, and he immediately spoils the compliment. Putting hell in the present tense makes the rest of the book an explanation: the reader knows the outcome and is waiting to be told what led to it.

quotations.text: Guess he’s been in Starkfield too many winters. Most of the smart ones get away.
quotations.speaker: Harmon Gow
quotations.context: The sentence the narrator says he built all his later inferences around.
quotations.analysis: Two flat statements which between them contain a theory of the whole district: that staying is what does the damage, and that staying is what the less able do. The narrator quotes it twice, and the second quotation is his admission that a reconstruction of twenty-four years has been grown from one man's offhand remark.

quotations.text: it seemed to produce no change except that of retarding still more the sluggish pulse of Starkfield
quotations.speaker: The narrator
quotations.context: The effect of a spell of bright clear cold on the village.
quotations.analysis: The village is given a pulse, which makes the winter a condition and the place a patient. It is the first of the book's many transfers of medical language away from Zeena, who is the only person in it with a diagnosis.

quotations.text: He seemed a part of the mute melancholy landscape, an incarnation of its frozen woe, with all that was warm and sentient in him fast bound below the surface; but there was nothing unfriendly in his silence.
quotations.speaker: The narrator
quotations.context: After several winter drives to the Junction in Frome's sleigh, in near-silence.
quotations.analysis: The man is absorbed into the scenery and then, in the last clause, handed back his humanity. ‘Fast bound below the surface’ describes ice over water, and the reconstruction that follows is an attempt to get at what is under it, an attempt the narrator has already told us is guesswork.

quotations.text: We’ll always go on living here together, and some day she’ll lie there beside me.
quotations.speaker: Ethan Frome
quotations.context: Walking Mattie home past the Frome graves, which had always oppressed him.
quotations.analysis: This is the novel's love scene, and it consists of a man imagining a shared grave. The graves that used to stand for everything he could not escape have been converted, in one sentence, into a promise — which tells the reader exactly how narrow the available happiness is.

quotations.text: There was in him a slumbering spark of sociability which the long Starkfield winters had not yet extinguished.
quotations.context: Ethan driving to the village in unusually good spirits, with Zeena away.
quotations.analysis: ‘Not yet’ is the word that makes a kind sentence threatening. The metaphor is a fire going out slowly in a cold house, and the chapter that contains it is the only one in which Ethan whistles, sings and behaves like a man of twenty-eight.

quotations.text: There the silence had deepened about him year by year.
quotations.context: The history of the farm after his father's accident and his mother's decline.
quotations.analysis: Silence is given a depth and a rate of increase, like snow or debt. The sentence also supplies the motive for the marriage twenty pages before the book states it: Ethan asks Zeena to stay because she has been speaking in a house where nobody spoke.

quotations.text: Sacred to the memory of Ethan Frome and Endurance his wife, who dwelled together in peace for fifty years.
quotations.context: An ancestor's headstone on the knoll, which had interested him as a boy because it bore his name.
quotations.analysis: The wife’s name is a virtue, and the epitaph is about how long they lasted: fifty years, in peace, together. Wharton then has Ethan wonder whether the same words will be written over him and Zeena, and the epilogue answers the question without needing a stone.

quotations.text: backed into the pickle-dish, which fell to the floor with a crash
quotations.context: The cat, startled off the table during the supper Ethan and Mattie have alone.
quotations.analysis: The agent of the disaster is a cat, which lets Wharton destroy the marriage's most valued object without giving anybody the blame or the satisfaction. The dish was a wedding present never used; taking it down for one meal is the only extravagance in the book, and it is punished within the hour.

quotations.text: I’ve got complications
quotations.speaker: Zeena Frome
quotations.context: Reporting the new Bettsbridge doctor's verdict, on her return.
quotations.analysis: Three words, delivered with the air of somebody singled out for a great fate. In a village where everybody has troubles, the word is a promotion, and Wharton has Zeena win the only argument that matters by producing a noun her husband cannot contradict.

quotations.text: To have them was in itself a distinction, though it was also, in most cases, a death-warrant.
quotations.context: The narrator explaining what the word means in that part of the country.
quotations.analysis: The sentence balances social promotion against a death sentence on either side of a comma, and ‘in most cases’ leaves room for the ones who live for decades. It is the book's one moment of open irony about Zeena, and it is also the book's refusal to say whether she is ill.

quotations.text: The doctor says it’ll be my death if I go on slaving the way I’ve had to.
quotations.speaker: Zeena Frome
quotations.context: Justifying the hired girl she has already engaged, which means Mattie must go.
quotations.analysis: The medical authority is quoted, never seen, and the word ‘slaving’ describes a household in which somebody else does the work. The sentence is unanswerable by design: to argue with it is to be a man who would rather keep a girl than keep his wife alive.

quotations.text: now you’ve took from me the one I cared for most of all
quotations.speaker: Zeena Frome
quotations.context: Holding the pieces of the red glass pickle-dish.
quotations.analysis: She is grieving over crockery, and the phrasing is that of a woman mourning a person — which is the nearest the novel lets her come to saying what she knows about her husband and her cousin. She then stops in a spasm of sobs and hardens again, and the marriage never discusses any of it.

quotations.text: He was a prisoner for life, and now his one ray of light was to be extinguished.
quotations.context: After the failure to raise fifty dollars from Andrew Hale.
quotations.analysis: The sentence comes straight after a page of arithmetic, the price of tickets, the mortgage, three months’ credit, so the prison metaphor is being checked against a ledger. Wharton is precise that the walls are financial, and that the door was shut by a kind man who was also short of money.

quotations.text: Right into the big elm. You said you could. So ’t we’d never have to leave each other any more.
quotations.speaker: Mattie Silver
quotations.context: At the top of the coast, after one run down, her lips against his ear.
quotations.analysis: She proposes it, not him, and she does so by quoting his own boast back at him. The reasoning in the last clause is a child's — this is the only way of not being separated — and the flat construction, with no word for death anywhere in it, is what makes the moment unbearable.

quotations.text: But suddenly his wife’s face, with twisted monstrous lineaments, thrust itself between him and his goal
quotations.context: The second run down the hill, with the elm ahead.
quotations.analysis: Zeena appears at the last possible instant as a hallucination and physically deflects the sled, so the crash that follows is neither a clean death nor a clean escape. Wharton has the marriage intervene in the accident itself, which is why the survivors end up in one kitchen and not in two graves.

quotations.text: A slatternly calico wrapper hung from her shoulders and the wisps of her thin grey hair were drawn away from a high forehead and fastened at the back by a broken comb.
quotations.context: The narrator's first sight of the woman who gets up to prepare the meal in the Frome kitchen.
quotations.analysis: The description is given before the name, so the reader spends a paragraph deciding which of the two women this is and gets it wrong. The broken comb is the detail that does the work: everything in the room has been mended once and is now simply being used broken.

quotations.text: And I say, if she’d ha’ died, Ethan might ha’ lived
quotations.speaker: Mrs Ned Hale
quotations.context: The impulse of complete avowal that seizes her after twenty-four years of reticence.
quotations.analysis: She has already said her minister was shocked by the same sentence, and she repeats it anyway, in dialect, with 'I say' at the front to mark that she knows what she is doing. It converts the accident from a tragedy into a failed mercy, which is a far harder thing for the reader to hold.

quotations.text: I don’t see’s there’s much difference between the Fromes up at the farm and the Fromes down in the graveyard; ’cept that down there they’re all quiet, and the women have got to hold their tongues.
quotations.speaker: Mrs Ned Hale
quotations.context: The last words of the book.
quotations.analysis: The joke is that the dead are quieter, and the sting is in what it concedes about the living: the kitchen is a grave with the arguing left in. Ending a novel about a man who could not speak on a line about women who cannot stop is Wharton's final adjustment to who, in Starkfield, has actually been silenced.

timeline.label: Edith Newbold Jones born in New York
timeline.detail: Into the old moneyed society she would spend a career anatomising.

timeline.label: Marriage to Edward Robbins Wharton
timeline.detail: A match that became increasingly unhappy and ended in divorce in 1913.

timeline.label: The Mount completed at Lenox, Massachusetts
timeline.detail: Wharton designed the house and gardens herself and lived in the Berkshire hill country this book is set in.

timeline.label: A coasting accident at Lenox
timeline.detail: A documented sledding accident in the town, often connected with the novel's ending, though Wharton did not identify it as her source.

timeline.label: Wharton's The House of Mirth published
timeline.detail: The novel that made her reputation, and the first of her studies of a woman destroyed by an economy she is not allowed to work in.

timeline.label: Ethan Frome published
timeline.detail: By Charles Scribner's Sons, after appearing in Scribner's Magazine.

timeline.label: Wharton's The Custom of the Country published
timeline.detail: Published two years later, and as ruthless about money in drawing rooms as this book is about money on a hill farm.

timeline.label: Wharton's The Age of Innocence published
timeline.detail: Written after the war, from France, looking back at the New York of her childhood.

timeline.label: Wharton wins the Pulitzer Prize for The Age of Innocence
timeline.detail: The first woman to receive it, for The Age of Innocence.

timeline.label: Wharton dies in France
timeline.detail: At Saint-Brice-sous-Forêt, north of Paris, where she had lived for years.

places.name: Lenox, Massachusetts
places.note: Where Wharton built The Mount and learned the Berkshire winters that Starkfield is made from.

places.name: Pittsfield, Massachusetts
places.note: The nearest real town of any size to Wharton's Berkshire country, and the model for the errands the Fromes take to Bettsbridge.

places.name: Mount Greylock
places.note: The highest point in Massachusetts, in the hill country whose isolated farms Wharton took her setting from.

places.name: Paris
places.note: Where Wharton was living when she wrote the French exercise, Hiver, that supplied the situation of this book.

places.name: New York
places.note: The city of Scribner's Magazine, which serialised the novella, and the society Wharton usually wrote about instead.

criticalViews.summary: On this reading the novel's subject is a household that cannot raise money: the unsellable farm, the three months' credit, the fifty dollars refused. Every emotional development is preceded by a financial one, and the ending is what happens when no exit can be paid for.
criticalViews.counter: It underrates how much of the trap Ethan builds himself — he has a letter written and abandons it before the money question is settled.

criticalViews.position: The frame as the novel's real subject
criticalViews.summary: Wharton gives an outsider nine chapters of confident access to a silent man's mind, having first told us his sources disagreed. Read this way the book is about how a village's reticence gets turned into a story, and about who is entitled to narrate a marriage.
criticalViews.counter: The reconstruction is so sustained and so intimate that most readers forget the frame entirely until the epilogue reopens it.

criticalViews.position: Zeena as the novel's misread figure
criticalViews.summary: Later criticism has argued that the one character denied an interior life is the one with the least power — a woman whose only available authority is illness, judged throughout by a narrator who met her once, and who is then found nursing the rival she dismissed.
criticalViews.counter: The epilogue's reversal may be less a rehabilitation than a final cruelty: all three are kept alive in one room precisely so that nobody is released.

criticalViews.position: New England realism against the pastoral
criticalViews.summary: Wharton said she was writing against the prettified rural New England of earlier fiction, and the novel's bareness — no charm, no folk wisdom, no redemptive nature — is a deliberate correction.
criticalViews.counter: The severity is itself a style, and the book's symmetry and symbolism are as shaped as anything it was reacting against.

essayQuestions.question: How far is the tragedy of Ethan Frome caused by poverty?
essayQuestions.focus: Money, obligation and the closing of every exit
plan: Collect the figures the novel is precise about: the mortgage, the unsold farm, three months' credit, fifty dollars, Mattie's fifty from her father.
Show how the plan to leave collapses in Chapter VIII on the price of the journey.
Weigh the competing cause: duty to a sick wife, and the sequence of invalids that began with Ethan's father.
Consider Mattie's position separately — her health broken by paid work, and no household but this one.
Decide whether the book presents poverty as the cause or as the thing that makes character irreversible.

essayQuestions.question: What does the framing narrator contribute to the novel?
essayQuestions.focus: Reconstruction, reliability and the limits of testimony
plan: Begin with the first sentence and its admission that the accounts did not agree.
Establish what the narrator could actually have learned, and from whom — Harmon Gow, Mrs Hale, one night in the kitchen.
Set that against the intimacy of the central chapters, which report Ethan's unspoken thoughts.
Examine the epilogue's reopening of the frame and the effect of hearing Mrs Hale's verdict in her own words.
Judge whether the frame undermines the story it introduces or gives it its authority.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss Wharton's presentation of Zeena.
essayQuestions.focus: Illness, power and the novel's silences
plan: Note that the reader never enters her mind, and ask who is responsible for that — Wharton, or the narrator she invented.
Trace the sequence by which illness becomes authority: the doctor at Bettsbridge, the word complications, the hired girl already engaged.
Read the pickle-dish scene as the only place her feeling reaches the surface, and consider what it is really about.
Use the epilogue, where she is on her feet and doing the nursing, to test every earlier judgement.
Conclude on whether the novel condemns her, pities her, or declines to decide.

essayQuestions.question: 'The most important thing in Ethan Frome is what the book does not narrate.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Silence, ellipsis and the gap before the epilogue
plan: List the unspoken: the unsent letter, the goodbye that is not said, Mrs Hale's twenty-four years of reticence.
Analyse the jump from the sled to the kitchen, and what the reader is required to construct across it.
Show how objects — a dish, a ribbon, a gravestone — carry the conversations the characters never have.
Consider the effect of putting the book's harshest statement in the mouth of its most reticent character, at the very end.
Assess what would be lost if the crash and its aftermath were narrated in full.

discussionQuestions: The narrator admits his sources contradicted each other. How much of the story should we believe?
Mattie proposes the crash, not Ethan. Does that change how you read her?
Zeena never gets a point of view. Is that Wharton's judgement on her, or the narrator's limitation?
The novel gives exact sums of money throughout. What would be different if it did not?
Mrs Hale says it would have been better if Mattie had died. Is the book agreeing with her?

related.why: Another short American novel about a marriage that offers no exit, published a decade earlier and equally unwilling to console.
The New England that Wharton was writing against and out of: small, watchful, and organised around what cannot be said.
A frame narrator piecing together a passion from other people's accounts, in a landscape that does half the work.
Rural poverty treated as a mechanism, not a backdrop, with the same refusal to let a good character escape.
Published fourteen years later, and also concerned with a life closed off by other people's care and the difference between surviving and living.
